snip.t: Deficiency arrests nuclear maturation → macrocytosis and megaloblastic changes. — Presence of hypersegmented neutrophils on the film and elevated methylmalonic acid helps the examiner differentiate B12 from folate deficiency.
Macrocytic: above 100 fL — Vitamin B12 or folate deficiency, alcohol, hypothyroidism, liver disease, drugs (zidovudine, methotrexate, hydroxycarbamide), myelodysplasia
| Vitamin B12/folate deficiency | Neurological signs, macrocytosis, dietary deficiency. | MCV ↑, hypersegmented neutrophils, normal iron studies, low B12/folate levels. |

Neurological: Numbness/tingling, gait instability, memory loss, mood change, depression, visual disturbances — Vitamin B12 deficiency (cobalamin) causes sub‑acute combined degeneration; folate deficiency may give mild neuro‑cognitive changes.
| Serum folate (red‑cell folate if available) | Folate stores | Low → folate‑deficiency; red‑cell folate reflects tissue stores better. |

| Tropical sprue | Recent travel to high‑altitude or coastal Kenya, chronic diarrhoea, folate deficiency, HIV co‑infection | Responds to tetracycline + folic acid; duodenal biopsy shows partial villous blunting |

qs.q: Which red cell distribution width (RDW) pattern is most commonly expected in nutritional deficiencies such as iron, vitamin B12, or folate deficiency?
o: A normal red cell distribution width
A very wide or elevated distribution width
qs.e: Nutritional deficiencies like iron, vitamin B12, or folate deficiency mostly present with an elevated RDW due to anisocytosis. If all cells are uniformly small or large, the RDW tends to remain normal or reduced.

qs.q: At what typical age do infants experience the peak incidence of megaloblastic anemia caused by folate deficiency?
o: Twelve to eighteen months of age
Three to five years of age
One to three weeks of age
Four to seven months of age
qs.e: Megaloblastic anemia from folate deficiency has its peak incidence at 4-7 months of age, somewhat earlier than iron-deficiency anemia. Infant body stores and rapid growth rates contribute to this window.

qs.q: What is the most common cause of folate deficiency in older children?
qs.e: Malnutrition is the most common cause of folate deficiency in older children, who are also at increased risk if they have hemoglobinopathies or infections. Intrinsic factor and ileal issues relate more to vitamin B12.

qs.q: What is the primary pathophysiological mechanism responsible for megaloblastic hematopoiesis in cobalamin or folate deficiency?
o: Disrupted DNA synthesis and ineffective hematopoiesis
Accelerated peripheral destruction of mature erythrocytes
Direct toxic suppression of marrow stem cell niches by metabolites
Massive hypersplenism leading to sequestration of precursors
qs.e: Megaloblastic hematopoiesis is characterized by marrow failure due to disrupted DNA synthesis and ineffective hematopoiesis, resulting in giant precursors. It is not caused by peripheral destruction or direct metabolite suppression.
